subject: Dedicated capacity sizing and peaking simulation for PulseTech go-live
messages:
From: Danielle Morris <danielle@pulsetech.io>
To: Evelyn Hart <evelyn_hart@redwood.ai>
Cc: Alex Chen <alex@pulsetech.io>
Date: 2027-04-04T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Dedicated capacity: production peaking and SLO fit (PulseTech pilot)

Evelyn —

Thanks for taking this. We're preparing our production plan for a Beta go-live in Q3 and procurement asked for concrete sizing and SLAs tied to committed capacity. I've attached our RFP and a traffic profile sheet that shows the synthetic and expected organic peaks over a 24-hour period. High level asks:

- A modeled tokens/sec requirement to meet our target throughput (we expect 600k tokens/day with bursts up to ~1.2M tokens in 10-15 minute windows).
- P95 latency target: <= 350ms for 128-token responses on our primary model.
- Recommended committed slab (GPU count + recommended burst allowance) and estimated percent-headroom.
- Fallback guidance (smaller model / quantization trade-offs) if we need to reduce committed spend.

Can you and your team run a short simulation and surface an initial recommendation this week? We're on a tight procurement cadence — legal and finance want a ballpark for the term sheet.

Attachments: PulseTech_RFP_Q1_2027.pdf, PT-Peak-Profile.xlsx

Cheers,
Danielle
Head of Platform Ops
PulseTech

From: Evelyn Hart <evelyn_hart@redwood.ai>
To: Danielle Morris <danielle@pulsetech.io>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
Date: 2027-04-05T11:05:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity: production peaking and SLO fit (PulseTech pilot)

Thanks Danielle — good packet, very clear. Brief reply with next steps and a provisional readout before the working session: 

1) Quick assumptions I used for the simulation (happy to change):
   - Primary model: rwd-7b-struct-v2 (fp16 baseline), average request = 128 tokens, mean response length 110 tokens.
   - Observed 10-15m burst windows from your sheet map to ~8 requests/sec aggregated across the fleet at peak.

2) Provisional throughput math (ballpark):
   - Baseline per-GPU sustained: ~520 tokens/sec (fp16 inference, batching enabled) for rwd-7b-struct-v2 on A100-class instance with our optimizations.
   - With smart batching + KV prefix caching we typically see 20-30% effective uplift on token throughput during well-patterned traffic.

3) Recommendation (initial):
   - To absorb the 15-minute burst and maintain P95 <= 350ms for 128T responses, plan committed slab = 10 GPUs, burst pool = +6 GPUs.
   - That maps to nominal sustained capacity ~10 * 520 = 5,200 tokens/sec, burst-capacity peak ~16 * 520 = 8,320 tokens/sec.
   - Given your expected daily tokens (600k) and short peaks, that equates to ~35-40% headroom in steady state with ~60% extra cushion for momentary peaking.

4) Options if you want to trade cost vs latency:
   - Quantized fp16->int8 variant (rwd-7b-q8) reduces per-token cost ~30% but lowers sustained tokens/sec by ~12% under heavy batching. Use as fall-through for non-critical routes.
   - Smaller model (rwd-3b) drops latency by ~10-15% on p95 at the expense of lower output quality for long-form prompts; good for high-volume low-complexity calls.

5) Next steps:
   - Karthik and Ben will run a deterministic simulation against your PT-Peak-Profile and return a 1-page slide with exact GPU counts, p95 projections, and cost delta for committed vs burst within 48 hours.
   - I'd like to schedule a 60-minute "peaking workshop" to walk procurement/eng through the assumptions and the runbook (proposed times attached in the calendar invite).

Folks — assigning Karthik and Ben to lead the compute simulation; they'll include a simple fallback decision tree we can fold into the term sheet.

Best,
Evelyn Hart
Director, Solutions — Redwood Inference
[Attachment: Runbook_Draft.md (text)]

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>
To: Evelyn Hart <evelyn_hart@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
Cc: Danielle Morris <danielle@pulsetech.io>
Date: 2027-04-06T09:20:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity: production peaking and SLO fit (PulseTech pilot)

Quick modeling notes (output from the simulation run attached as slide snippets in the drive link):

Assumptions (detailed):
- Model: rwd-7b-struct-v2 (baseline), rwd-7b-q8 (quantized fallback), rwd-3b (low-cost fallback).
- Hardware profile: A100-40GB equivalents; 1 GPU sustained compute profile = 520 tokens/sec @ p95 approx 280ms for 128T when batching factor varies 8-24.
- Cold-start penalty: 70-120ms for cold KV cache; mitigations via warm routes and prefix cache.
- Traffic mix: 78% synchronous low-latency requests, 22% background batch generation (ok to schedule on lower priority).

Key results (rounded):
- Steady-state (daily avg) demand -> ~7.0K tokens/sec sustained equivalent across 24h (this includes background).
- Peak 15-min window -> modeled 1.1M tokens over 15m = ~1,220 tokens/sec sustained during window. Note: your sheet numbers map to 1.05-1.3M across scenarios.

Sizing & SLO fit: 
- To meet P95 <= 350ms for 128T: committed slab = 6 GPUs (handles baseline sustained with 20% margin on baseline traffic) + reserved burst pool = 8 GPUs.
- Operationally, we recommend committing to 8 GPUs for a conservative SLA (gives ~30% steady-headroom) and enabling short-term burst to 14 GPUs for scheduled peak windows.
- Why different from Evelyn's quick read: Evelyn took a conservative per-GPU floor. My sim added traffic-shaping (route-level prioritization) and lower batch efficiency during unpredictable bursts which lowered per-GPU effective throughput in worst-case; hence the slight delta.

Headroom:
- Committed = 8 GPUs -> steady headroom ~28-35% depending on request clustering.
- Burst to 14 GPUs -> headroom during peak ~80-85% above steady committed capacity, which comfortably covers the modeled 15-min windows.

Trade-offs summary for procurement:
- Commit 8 GPUs monthly: lower overall committed-cost; requires orchestration to rapidly spin burst to cover quote windows.
- Commit 12 GPUs monthly: reduces complexity on scaling and reduces 95th percentile risk for highly bursty days — recommended if PulseTech wants a simpler SLAs and lower ops burden.

I'll attach the CSV output from the simulator to the Drive folder and tag the key lines in the slide doc. Evelyn / Danielle — happy to walk through the micro assumptions in the workshop.

—Karthik
Principal Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: Danielle Morris <danielle@pulsetech.io>
To: Evelyn Hart <evelyn_hart@redwood.ai>
Cc: Alex Chen <alex@pulsetech.io>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>
Date: 2027-04-07T16:33:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity: production peaking and SLO fit (PulseTech pilot)

Evelyn / Karthik — this is great, thanks. Procurement and finance are aligned to move forward with a narrow-term committed slab but want two options in the SOW:

1) Option A (lower commit): 8 GPUs committed + burst up to 14 GPUs.
2) Option B (higher commit): 12 GPUs committed with smaller burst pool (up to 16 GPUs) and a 10% discount on committed capacity.

Questions we still have before the SOW draft:
- Can you provide the expected delta in monthly $ between A and B (ballpark $/month) including burst usage assumptions?
- For Option A, what happens operationally if we see sustained multi-hour peaks (what's the fail-safe to avoid p95 > 350ms)?

Can we do the 60-minute workshop tomorrow 2027-04-08 at 10:00 PT? We'll have procurement, platform, and one of our SREs on the call. Also please send a brief runbook excerpt that we can attach to the SOW describing fallback decision tree (model-downscale -> quantized path -> degraded-quality alerting).

If everything looks good we'll route a draft SOW to DocuSign (I pasted the link in related_links).

Best,
Danielle
Head of Platform Ops, PulseTech
